reading.body:
The dataset layer of AI breaks into three parts, and the smallest of them by count is training data.

Training datasets number 8, evaluation datasets 9, and licensing and provenance 17. The legal and provenance questions outnumber the technical ones roughly two to one. That ratio is the useful signal here: what may lawfully be used, and how to tell, is the most populated part of this map.

For AI specifically, this matters because datasets are the input that compute consumes. A model's scale is bounded by the corpus it was trained on, and the licence attached to that corpus decides whether the training run can happen at all. Provenance is not paperwork around the compute story, it is a gate in front of it.

The data does not say how large any corpus is, how many languages it covers, or what bias has been documented in it, despite those being named as the dimensions of interest. It gives counts of entries, not measurements of the datasets themselves. Nothing here speaks to power, buildings, or siting, and it should not be read as doing so.
